title: Old Wisdom. New Science.
intro: Long ago, wise people in India asked the biggest questions in life: Who am I? Why am I here? How can I be truly happy? Their answers are still with us. Dr. Hari Krishna explains them in plain words, puts them next to what science knows today, and shows how to use them in daily life. You don't need any background — just curiosity.

cards.title: India's Old Books, Made Simple
cards.body: India has some of the oldest wisdom books in the world — like the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita. Dr. Hari Krishna takes their big ideas and explains them like a friend would: why we feel what we feel, how our actions come back to us (karma), what is right to do (dharma), and who we really are inside.

cards.title: Great Teachers, One Message
cards.body: Many great teachers — the Buddha, Adi Shankaracharya, Swami Vivekananda, Ramana Maharshi and others — lived in different times and places. Yet they pointed to the same things: a calm mind, kind actions, and knowing yourself. Dr. Hari Krishna shows what each of them can teach us today.

cards.title: What Science Says
cards.body: Can science explain why meditation works? Today, doctors and scientists study how a calm mind changes the brain, our health and our moods. Dr. Hari Krishna puts these findings side by side with the old teachings — so you can understand them, not just believe them.

riverStory: A little boy once asked his grandfather, “Thatha, where do we go when we die?” The grandfather smiled: “To heaven, if we do good.” “But where is heaven, Thatha?” The grandfather had no answer — and the question stayed with the boy.
riverIntro: Wise people in India lived with questions like that for over three thousand years. Their answers became famous books: the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, the Bhagavad Gita and the Puranas. Most of us have heard these names, but not how they fit together. Here is the simple secret: they are not separate books. They are like one river, starting as a small spring in the mountains and flowing all the way to the sea. Let's walk along it, one stop at a time.

questions.label: about the world
questions.title: What is this world?
questions.body: Where did everything come from? What keeps it going? Is it real, or like a dream? Will it end — and how am I connected to it?

questions.label: about yourself
questions.title: Who am I, really?
questions.body: Who am I, beyond my name and my body? Where did I come from, and where am I going? What is my life for, and how do I find a happiness that lasts?

questionsNote: These two questions started the river. Every stop below answers them in its own way.

stages.place: Stop 1 · The spring in the mountains
stages.name: The Vedas
stages.body: The Vedas are India's oldest songs, thousands of years old. The wise people who received them — called rishis — said they didn't make them up. They heard them, sitting in silence in forests and by rivers. That is why the Vedas are called Shruti, “what was heard.” And one of the first things they asked was a question full of wonder: what was there before anything existed?
stages.verse: Nāsad āsīn no sad āsīt tadānīm
stages.meaning: In the beginning, there was neither something nor nothing.
stages.tryThis: Close your eyes for two minutes and just listen to every sound, near and far, without naming them. Simply listening was the very first practice.

stages.name: The Upanishads
stages.body: Next, the river became quiet and deep. In small forest schools, teachers sat close to their students and talked softly. The question changed. Instead of “What is the world?” they asked, “Who is the one asking?” Looking outside turned into looking inside.
stages.meaning: What makes the mind think and move?
stages.tryThis: The next time a thought comes up, gently ask: “Who is noticing this thought?” Don't try to answer — just look.

stages.place: Stop 3 · The river gets its banks
stages.name: Remembered teachings
stages.body: Something that is only heard can be forgotten. So the wise people remembered these teachings and wrote them down in simpler words, as guides for everyday life — how to live well in a family and a community. These are called Smriti, “what was remembered.” They are the bridge from the forest to our homes.
stages.verse: Śrutis tu vedo vijñeyo dharma-śāstraṁ tu vai smṛtiḥ
stages.meaning: What was heard is the Veda; what was remembered is the guide to right living.
stages.tryThis: Think of one good habit or value your grandparents lived by. Try living by it once today.

stages.name: The great stories
stages.alias: Ramayana & Mahabharata — wisdom you can see
stages.body: Now the river reached ordinary people — through stories. The Ramayana shows how to live a good life through Rama. The Mahabharata shows how to think when right and wrong are not clear. Big ideas became people you could know and love.
stages.meaning: The great stories are like a fifth Veda — for everyone.
stages.tryThis: Facing a hard choice this week? Ask yourself what is the right thing to do — not just the easy thing.

stages.name: The Bhagavad Gita
stages.body: On a battlefield, a great warrior named Arjuna is so upset that he drops his bow and cries. In that dark moment, his friend and guide Krishna talks to him. Their conversation — the Gita — puts the best of all the old teachings into 18 short chapters. A crisis didn't stop the river. It made it deeper.
stages.meaning: The real you is never born and never dies.
stages.tryThis: Do one task today with all your attention — and then let go of worrying about how it turns out.

stages.name: The Puranas
stages.body: At last the river split into a thousand small streams and reached every village. The Puranas are collections of stories, songs and festivals. A temple in every village, a story in every temple — and in every story, the same water. What only scholars understood before, now reached every heart.
stages.meaning: We think about the highest truth.
stages.tryThis: Pick one name of God or one word that brings you peace, and repeat it quietly for five minutes. No hurry.

riverEnd: And where does the river end? In the ocean — and that ocean is your own heart. The whole journey was flowing toward you.
ghatsIntro: A river has many ghats — steps leading down to the water — but the water is the same. The river doesn't care which steps you use. Start wherever you are today.

ghats.who: If you like to do things
ghats.text: The Vedas give a short prayer, the Gayatri:
ghats.meaning: May that light make our thinking clear.

ghats.who: If you like to ask questions
ghats.text: The Upanishads give a famous saying:
ghats.meaning: You are that — what you are looking for is in you.

ghats.who: If you have a family to care for
ghats.text: Rama's life shows how to live well, and the Mahabharata shows how to make hard choices.

ghats.who: If you are going through a hard time
ghats.verse: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana
ghats.meaning: Your effort is in your hands — the result is not.

ghats.who: If you are led by your heart
ghats.text: The Puranas give the way of love — listening to the stories, singing the names, and letting your heart open.

closingMeaning: Truth is one; wise people describe it in many ways.
closingBody: Because people are different, the ways had to be many — that is not confusion, it is kindness. Think of a mother: she sings to her baby, tells stories to her child and gives advice to her grown son. The words change; the love doesn't. These are not six separate books on a shelf. They are six rooms in one home — and that home is you.
sourceNote: Based on the Telugu study “Bharatiya Jnana Parampara — from the Vedas to the Puranas, one living river.” Read the books yourself, learn from a good teacher, and let one simple line walk with you every day.
libraryTitle: Explore the Golden Age Wisdom Library
libraryBody: We are building one simple place where anyone can learn about India's wisdom books, the great teachers and different ways of thinking — explained clearly, without difficult words. Dr. Hari Krishna's talks and our learning resources are free for everyone.
libraryCloseSub: One place to learn wisdom from around the world.
